category_title: Preschoolers who cry when encountering perceived difficult tasks
minimal_context: Zeke is getting ready for recess and needs to put on his coat in Mr. Cho's class.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Zeke, it is time for recess. Please put on your coat.

STUDENT: (Looks at the coat and begins to whine) It's too hard.

TUTOR: Just give it a try.

STUDENT: (Struggles with the sleeve and starts crying softly)

TUTOR: Keep working on it, you need your coat to go outside.

STUDENT: (Drops the coat and cries loudly, with the crying episode lasting for over 77 seconds)

options.A: Listen and support Zeke's needs through shared power by compromising, negotiating situations, or sharing decisions with him instead of trying to impose control over his behaviors during the coat routine.
options.B: Provide a clear beginning and end for each task, such as putting on his coat, during the arrival, recess, and dismissal routines in Mr. Cho's class.
options.C: Address Zeke's feelings mutually rather than repressing them, allowing for the exploration of his disappointments and constraints when he struggles with putting on his coat.
options.D: Provide a visual prompt mounted above Zeke's coat hook at school and on the wall at home that includes pictures of the steps for putting on or taking off his clothes and asking for help.
